name: Law of Prägnanz
description: When several organizations are possible, perception tends to settle on the simplest, most stable overall form the stimulus supports. Designers invoke it when reducing clutter helps people 'see the pattern' faster.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to iconography, diagramming, layout simplification, chart styling, and reducing ambiguous compositions so screens read as clear structures rather than noisy fragments.
prevalence_note: Regularly taught anywhere Gestalt principles are taught, especially in visual- and interaction-design fundamentals, but referenced less often in everyday product critique than proximity or similarity.

findings.description: Wagemans et al.'s companion review treats the law of Prägnanz directly as the tendency toward the simplest possible organization permitted by the available stimulation, and argues that contemporary vision science provides four substantive foundations for that idea: self-organization dynamics, neural-resource economy, Bayesian optimality, and structural information theory.
findings.source_title: A century of Gestalt psychology in visual perception: II. Conceptual and theoretical foundations.

applications.title: The Olympic rings and the WWF panda: reading a handful of simple shapes as one coherent, meaningful whole
applications.description: The Interaction Design Foundation's reference article on the Law of Prägnanz (published August 31, 2016) names the Olympic rings and the World Wildlife Fund's panda logo as direct illustrations of the principle: five overlapping circles, or a handful of black shapes with no continuous outline, are perceived immediately as one coherent, meaningful form rather than as a set of disconnected fragments -- the mind settling on the simplest, most stable interpretation the stimulus supports, exactly as the Law of Prägnanz predicts. The same article separately points to Google's search homepage (minimal layout, a single prominent search bar, heavy negative space) as an interface-level application of the same underlying preference for the simplest legible structure.
applications.industry_context: Logo and brand-identity design generally, spanning sport (Olympics), nonprofit (WWF), and technology (Google) branding.
applications.ethical_note: A pure visual-perception design principle with no persuasive or manipulative dimension -- the goal is legibility and memorability, not steering a decision the viewer wouldn't otherwise make.
